items.text: Orthostatic vitals: SBP drop >=20 / DBP >=10 mmHg or pulse increment >=30/min at 1-3 min standing

ask.changes_what: A positive exposure history should lead to stopping or dose-adjusting the agent, avoiding further nephrotoxins and monitoring creatinine; still assess obstruction and volume status.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not attribute AKI solely to a drug or contrast when there is oliguria, sepsis, hypotension or possible obstruction; these still need evaluation.
ask.escalation_warning: AKI with hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uremic symptoms needs urgent nephrology review regardless of the exposure history.
ask.how: Reconcile all drugs against the chart and pharmacy record, including over-the-counter NSAIDs and herbal products: NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, diuretics, aminoglycosides, vancomycin (with piperacillin-tazobactam), PPIs, and any iodinated contrast. For each, record start date, dose change and timing relative to the creatinine rise.
ask.negative_finding: No exposure lowers the likelihood of drug-related AKI and contrast nephropathy, redirecting attention to hypovolemia, sepsis, obstruction and intrinsic renal disease.
ask.pitfalls: Patients under-report OTC NSAIDs; PPI-associated AIN can begin weeks to months after the start; contrast-associated AKI is often confounded by the illness that prompted imaging, so timing alone does not prove causation.
ask.positive_finding: A nephrotoxin started or dosed within days of the creatinine rise, or contrast within 48-72 h, makes drug-induced AKI (hemodynamic, ATN or AIN) a leading candidate and identifies an immediately reversible factor.
ask.prerequisites: Access to medication administration and imaging records; collateral history for patients who cannot report OTC use.
ask.rationale: NSAID use and other nephrotoxins are common causes of AKI and stopping them can prevent further injury.
ask.title: Nephrotoxin and contrast exposure history (NSAID, ACEi/ARB, diuretic, aminoglycoside, vancomycin, PPI, iodinated contrast; timing)

ask.changes_what: Positive: stop the suspect drug, check urinalysis for pyuria/WBC casts and consider biopsy/steroids early; negative should not remove AIN from the differential of unexplained AKI on a new drug.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of fever/rash/arthralgia to exclude AIN, especially with PPIs or NSAIDs; do not attribute fever plus AKI to AIN without considering sepsis.
ask.escalation_warning: Rapidly rising creatinine, oliguria, or hyperkalemia on a suspect drug needs same-day nephrology review; biopsy decisions are time-sensitive because delayed drug withdrawal worsens recovery.
ask.how: Take a dated medication history for the preceding weeks to months (antibiotics, PPIs, NSAIDs, allopurinol, immune checkpoint inhibitors) and ask about fever, new rash, joint pains, and flank pain since starting; inspect the skin. Correlate the time course with the onset of creatinine rise.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of the triad is the rule: in biopsy series each feature is present in fewer than half of cases and the full triad in roughly 10%, so absence does not lower the probability of AIN meaningfully.
ask.pitfalls: PPI- and NSAID-induced AIN are typically oligosymptomatic with long latency; fever and rash after a new drug also occur with drug fever, DRESS, and infection without AIN. Definitive diagnosis requires kidney biopsy.
ask.positive_finding: Fever, rash, or arthralgia emerging after a new drug in a patient with unexplained AKI (often with sterile pyuria) supports drug-induced AIN and should prompt stopping the drug and nephrology input.
ask.prerequisites: Complete drug list including over-the-counter and recently stopped agents.
ask.rationale: AIN is a possible cause of AKI in the setting of new drugs, and the triad can prompt early drug cessation and further workup.
ask.title: Rash, fever, arthralgia after new drug (AIN triad)

examine.changes_what: Positive → catheterize/measure PVR now and seek the cause (drugs, prostate, cauda equina); negative with risk factors → bladder scan.
examine.contraindications: Avoid deep palpation over fresh lower abdominal incisions.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use an absent suprapubic mass to exclude retention in AKI, delirium or suspected cauda equina — measure post-void residual.
examine.escalation_warning: Retention with new saddle anesthesia, leg weakness or back pain → emergent cauda equina evaluation (MRI).
examine.how: Patient supine: percuss from the umbilicus toward the pubis for a dome of suprapubic dullness and palpate for a smooth, tense, tender midline mass rising from the pelvis that provokes urge. Ask about LUTS, straining, dribbling, hematuria, prostate disease, anticholinergic/opioid use and time since last void; confirm with bladder scan or catheter volume.
examine.negative_finding: A non-palpable bladder does not exclude retention: obesity, smaller volumes and silent postoperative or opioid-related distension are missed. Obtain a bladder scan or post-void residual when retention is plausible.
examine.pitfalls: Postoperative bladder volume >500 mL was present in 44% at recovery-room discharge, and 54% of those without symptoms of distension could not void within 30 min (PMID 14977795, Abstract). Pelvic masses, pregnancy and ascites mimic; palpation cannot estimate volume.
examine.positive_finding: A palpable or percussible bladder above the pubis with inability to void indicates retention — catheterize and measure volume. This is a treatable cause of AKI, delirium and abdominal pain.
examine.prerequisites: Attempt to void first when able; know time of last void.
examine.rationale: Detecting a distended bladder would immediately prompt catheterization for suspected retention/obstruction, a leading cause of anuria.
examine.title: Suprapubic palpation / percussion for distended bladder; LUTS and prostate history

examine.changes_what: Positive: emergency MRI whole lumbosacral spine/urgent spinal surgical referral. Negative: does not exclude cauda equina; if suspicion persists (bilateral sciatica, retention) still image.
examine.contraindications: Patient refusal; rectal exam may be deferred if imaging is already being obtained emergently, but perineal sensation should still be tested.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use normal anal tone or perineal sensation to defer imaging when bilateral sciatica, new urinary retention or incontinence is present; the exam is insensitive for early cauda equina.
examine.escalation_warning: Any new saddle sensory change, sphincter disturbance or retention with back pain is a surgical emergency: emergent MRI and spinal referral without waiting for full deficit.
examine.how: With a chaperone and consent, test light touch and pinprick over the perineum, perianal skin, buttocks and inner thighs (S2-S5) comparing sides and asking about numbness when wiping; then digital rectal examination assessing resting anal tone, voluntary squeeze, and perianal sensation/anal wink. Pair with a bladder scan for post-void residual.
examine.negative_finding: Normal perineal sensation and anal tone do not exclude cauda equina compression - pooled sensitivities of individual red flags are only 0.19-0.43, and the diagnosis is often early or incomplete when sphincter signs are absent.
examine.pitfalls: Subjective perineal numbness is more sensitive than objective testing; anal tone is unreliable with prior anorectal surgery, chronic constipation or in the elderly. A large post-void residual (>500 mL) is the single most predictive bedside finding and should be checked with the exam.
examine.positive_finding: New saddle sensory loss or reduced anal tone in a patient with back pain and bilateral leg or sphincter symptoms is a red flag that mandates emergency MRI; pooled red flags for MRI-confirmed cauda equina are more specific (0.62-0.88) than sensitive.
examine.prerequisites: Chaperone, explanation and consent; document time of onset of bladder/bowel symptoms and bilateral leg symptoms.
examine.rationale: Finding saddle anesthesia or reduced anal tone would prompt urgent imaging for cauda equina, a rare but critical cause of retention.
examine.title: Saddle (perineal) sensory loss and reduced anal tone

examine.changes_what: Elevated JVP moves dyspnea/edema toward acute HF or RV/pericardial disease and away from hypovolemia; a flat JVP in hypotension favors hypovolemia/sepsis over cardiogenic causes.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid firm neck pressure in patients with carotid disease.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal JVP to withhold treatment for suspected heart failure, or declare a shocked patient hypovolemic when the neck cannot be adequately examined (obesity, short neck, column above the jaw).
examine.escalation_warning: Elevated JVP with hypotension, clear lungs and tachycardia suggests tamponade, RV infarction or massive PE and needs immediate echo/POCUS rather than diuresis.

evidence.citation: Butman SM, Ewy GA, Standen JR, Kern KB, Hahn E. Bedside cardiovascular examination in patients with severe chronic heart failure: importance of rest or inducible jugular venous distension. J Am Coll Cardiol 1993;22(4):968-74.
evidence.population: 52 patients with severe chronic heart failure undergoing in-hospital transplant evaluation; index finding = jugular venous distension at rest OR inducible by the abdominojugular test
evidence.quote: had the best combination of sensitivity (81%), specificity (80%) and predictive accuracy (81%) for elevation of the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
evidence.target_condition: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (>=18 mmHg)

evidence.citation: Signs and symptoms in adult patients with acute dyspnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Emerg Med 2018;25(1):3-11 (author list not retrievable via abstract tool; confirmed by PMID/DOI).
evidence.population: Adults with a new episode of acute dyspnea; 8 ED studies, 4737 patients; HF prevalence 25-59%
evidence.quote: Elevated jugular venous pressure (0.88, pooled odds ratio: 7), added third heart sound (0.97), and lung crepitations (0.77, pooled odds ratio: 11)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of HF per included studies (varied)
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure as cause of acute dyspnea

evidence.citation: Mant J, Doust J, Roalfe A, et al. Systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis of diagnosis of heart failure, with modelling of implications of different diagnostic strategies in primary care. Health Technol Assess 2009;13(32):1-207.
evidence.population: Patients with suspected heart failure in primary care; individual patient data meta-analysis of 9 studies
evidence.quote: orthopnoea (89%), oedema (72%), elevated jugular venous pressure (70%), cardiomegaly (85%), added heart sounds (99%), lung crepitations (81%)
evidence.reference_standard: Echocardiography / expert panel per included studies
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (new diagnosis) in primary care

examine.how: Recline the patient at 30-45 degrees (adjust until the top of the pulsation is visible), turn the head slightly left, and use tangential light to find the top of the internal jugular column. Measure its vertical height above the sternal angle; >3 cm above the angle (about >8 cm H2O total) is elevated.
examine.negative_finding: A flat or normal JVP lowers but does not exclude heart failure; sensitivity is modest (roughly 0.2-0.7 across ED studies) and pooled sensitivity in ED series stays below 0.55.
examine.pitfalls: Confusing carotid with venous pulsation, misjudging the sternal angle-to-atrium distance (varies with position), and failing to see a very high column (look for earlobe pulsation) or a very low one (lie the patient flatter). Isolated RV failure, tricuspid disease, tamponade or constriction raise JVP without left-sided congestion.
examine.positive_finding: A venous column >3 cm above the sternal angle indicates raised right atrial pressure and, in chronic heart failure, usually raised left-sided filling pressure (PCWP >=18 mmHg). It substantially raises the probability of heart failure as the cause of acute dyspnea.
examine.prerequisites: Adequate light, exposed neck, patient relaxed and breathing quietly; identify the venous (biphasic, non-palpable, falls with inspiration, occludable) rather than carotid pulsation.
examine.rationale: JVP assessment helps distinguish between hypovolemia, cardiorenal, and other causes of AKI, guiding fluid or diuretic management.
examine.title: Jugular venous pressure elevated (>8 cm H2O / >3 cm above sternal angle); low/flat JVP as the negative

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant hypovolemia/bleeding or medication-related OH and act; negative: large blood loss unlikely, but moderate loss still possible.
examine.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is frankly hypotensive, has an unstable spine/pelvis, or cannot safely bear weight.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing measurements in a patient who is already hypotensive, too dizzy or weak to stand safely, or has an unstable spine or pelvis; a patient too dizzy to stand counts as a positive test.
examine.escalation_warning: A positive test in a patient with possible bleeding indicates large volume loss and should trigger resuscitation and source search, not observation.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.target_condition: Large acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.target_condition: Moderate acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy
evidence.quote: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent, even after up to 1150 mL of blood loss (sensitivity, 33%; 95% CI, 21%-47%, for supine hypotension)
evidence.target_condition: Blood loss up to 1150 mL - supine hypotension (comparator finding, not postural)

examine.how: Measure BP and pulse after >=2 min supine, then have the patient stand and repeat at 1 and 3 min (standing, not sitting). Record SBP fall >=20 or DBP fall >=10 mmHg, pulse rise >=30/min, and whether the patient is too dizzy to stand (count that as positive).
examine.negative_finding: A normal postural pulse response argues strongly against large blood loss (LR- about 0.03) but misses most moderate (450-630 mL) losses (sensitivity 22%). Normal orthostatics do not exclude hypovolemia from vomiting/diarrhea.
examine.pitfalls: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent even after 1 L blood loss. Beta-blockers blunt the pulse response; sitting instead of standing lowers sensitivity; mild postural dizziness alone has no proven value.
examine.positive_finding: A postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness is highly specific (98%) for blood loss and is nearly always present after large (>1 L) hemorrhage. In an older patient with syncope, an SBP fall >=20 mmHg reproducing symptoms supports orthostatic hypotension, though asymptomatic falls are common with age and medications.
examine.prerequisites: Automated or manual cuff, an assistant to steady the patient, supine rest of at least 2 minutes first.
examine.rationale: Orthostatic vitals help identify hypovolemia as a cause of AKI and guide immediate fluid resuscitation if positive.
examine.title: Orthostatic vitals: SBP drop >=20 / DBP >=10 mmHg or pulse increment >=30/min at 1-3 min standing
